Objectives: The objective of this project is to reestablish vegetation conditions conducive to sage grouse reoccupation of an historic strutting ground (i.e., a site for communal reproductive display). Mature basin big sagebrush canopies have progressively impinged on the small meadow that was used for lekking and it is likely that these conditions currently deter potential use of the site. Successful reoccupation of this strutting ground, approximately 1/4 mile from the most current lek located on Rio Blanco County Road 3, would help separate road-related disruption of sage grouse reproductive activities and allow\r\nExxonMobil unimpeded use of this county road for natural gas development during the birds\u2019 reproductive timeframes (March through May).
Planned_Implementation:
ExxonMobil has offered to perform this work in conjunction with nearby brush clearing
operations (October 2004). A form of brushbeater called a rotary axe would be used to remove
basin big sagebrush from a 3-acre area surrounding the historic sage grouse lek. The rotary axe
is a self-propelled, rubber tired vehicle with a brush-beating head attached to an extendable arm
(similar to a backhoe). Utah serviceberry and basin big sagebrush canopies would be removed to
within 8” of the ground surface while leaving shrub regeneration and the herbaceous understory
undisturbed. There are no plans to alter livestock management or distribution on the project
area. Since these treatment techniques do not involve notable soil disturbance, there are no plans
to introduce supplement seed on treatment areas.

Objectives:
Reduce hazardous fuels adjacent to wildland/urban interface areas of Price, Helper, and Kenilworth and within the Coal Creek Watershed.  Reduce risks of a continued fire hazard due to a buildup of fuels, loss of big game habitat and forage from the encroachment of pinyon and juniper into this range habitat and a threat to public and firefighter safety in the event of a wildfire event.
The project goal would be to reduce fuel load and continuity in this wildland-urban
interface, decreasing the catastrophic fire potential.  The end result of the project
would be to leave trees scattered across the area to more closely resemble a naturally
occurring mosaic.
Planned_Implementation:
Trees and heavy brush to be removed would be selected based on hazardous potential as
well as retention of the existing character of the landscape. Lower branches of trees
remaining within the fuel break area would be pruned to four feet above ground level to
remove vertical continuity and encourage growth of grass understory. Where flat terrain
is easily accessible, a mechanical chipper/shredder (bullhog) would be utilized to remove
hazardous fuels and achieve treatment goals.

Leave islands of untreated vegetation (1-3 acres each) are scattered throughout the project area to provide additional wildlife cover. Additional\r\nsmall clumps of trees (10-15 foot) were also left throughout much of the project area\r\nrather than single leave trees.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results: Successfully achieved treatment goals would result in an open, park-like area with stands of vegetation in mosaic patterns throughout the project area. All woody surface materials and ladder fuels considered to have hazardous fuel potential\r\nwould be cleared.

Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
2011 Monitoring Report: Executive Summary
Tamarisk reduction along the Colorado River within the Moab Field Office BLM has been fairly successful. Pre-treatment tamarisk cover was 90-100% cover and has been successfully reduced to between 10-30% depending on the removal technique. From a fire and fuels perspective, the objective of creating and maintaining fuel breaks along the river has been successful. However, the invasion of secondary weeds has been nearly ubiquitous to these tamarisk treatments and there are still a greater amount of invasive weeds than native species. This has illustrated that our ecological restoration goals have not yet been achieved. Primary weed species, other than tamarisk, include Russian knapweed, Kochia, Cheatgrass, and Lambsquarter.
It is probable that the both the tamarisk beetle and these secondary weeds are helping to reduce the amount of tamarisk resprouting and growth as well as the recovery of native species. However, the extent of this competitive influence is still unclear.
Several notable patterns have emerged and are listed below. It will, however, require additional replication to validate these patterns.
Early spring broadcast burn unit has the most native species and the highest cottonwood density. Hot midsummer broadcast burn has the most even ratio of exotic to native species but has less diversity and one less growing season of data. Knapweed had the greatest cover in areas with intense fire on the ground. In particular, when bullhog chips were “underburned” in a wildfire. Knapweed may be inhibited by layer of bullhog chips. Kochia prevalent everywhere but peaks in the second growing season. Kochia is lowest in areas of least soil disturbance (i.e. hand pile). Cheatgrass prevalent in hand pile and bullhog areas. Cheatgrass thrives in areas with litter and both hand pile and bullhog units have the most remnant litter. Lambsquarter is a minor component which seems to thin over time. Broadcast burn areas have the most native recovery and predominately from shrub resprouting and cottonwood seedlings.

Treatment Prescription for Hand cut, Pile, Pile Burn, without Herbicide
The goals of this treatment are wildfire hazard reduction by cutting, piling and covering green and dead Tamarisk and Russian olive trees. Leave trees are identified as any species other than Tamarisk or Russian olive. Green and dead Tamarisk and Russian olive trees throughout all treatment units are completely severed from the stump(s). However, some of the larger Russian olive trees are left on site as wildlife trees. In these cases, the trees are girdled to kill the tree and create a snag for habitat. No live or dead limbs are left on the stumps of cut trees. Stump height is a minimum of 6 inches but does not exceed 12 inches measured on the uphill side. All main branches or stems are cut from the trunk of the tree to meet piling criteria. Materials not piled are bucked or cut into lengths is not to exceed 4 feet.
Piles are approximately 6 feet by 6 feet in size. All cut and existing dead and down slash between one and seven inches in diameter and greater than 2 feet in length is piled. All natural openings are used before clearing a pile site. Piles are not located within 10 feet of the unit boundary or road system. Piles are covered with 4 mil black plastic sheeting and are of a minimum size of 6? X 6? or large enough to cover a minimum of 80% of the pile volume to prevent moisture from getting into the piled wood. Where possible, piles are not placed on stumps in order to facilitate follow-up herbicide application although no herbicide was applied in these treatment areas.
Piles are burned in November, December, January, February, and March using single and double entry drip torch passes. Piles are burned in such a way as to minimize the scorching of leave trees.
Treatment Prescription for Hand cut, Pile, Pile Burn, with Herbicide
This treatment is the same as above except for the application of herbicide. Unlike other manual treatments where stump height of cut vegetation is six inches or less, when an area dominated with tamarisk is to receive an herbicide application, cut vegetation is “high stumped” leaving approximately twelve inches of stump height. After the piled slash is burned, hand crews reenter the treatment area to “low stump” or cut remaining stumps as flush to the ground as possible followed with an immediate herbicide application to the stumps. Herbicides are applied to each cut stump within 15 minutes of treatment. The advantages to this approach are that it is much easier to flush cut and apply herbicide to the stumps once the slash is removed. Additionally, the number of personnel exposed to the herbicide is reduced. Three distinct herbicide treatments are applied in most cases. The first is a basal bark spray applied to Tamarisk resprouts. Basal bark treatments are comprised of 25% Garlon 4 in a Methylated seed oil or JLB oil and are typically applied in fall or winter. Objectives:
The goal of treating dense mixed conifer is to reduce the fuel hazard while restoring
ecosystem health by re-establishing the natural variability, stability, and diversity of the
vegetative community within the project area. In designing a specific fuel treatment
prescription, techniques for reducing crown fire occurrence and severity may include ( 1)
increasing canopy base height, (2) reducing canopy bulk density, (3) reducing forest
canopy continuity and ( 4) reducing surface fuels.
Planned_Implementation:
Proposed treatment activities would involve hand cutting and piling; hand cutting with
lopping and scattering of slash; machine mastication, prescribed fire, fence construction
and kiosk installation. Woody surface materials and ladder fuels considered to have
hazardous fuel potential would be cleared and scattered.
There are several drainages within the collective project boundary in which treatment
methods may be modified to protect prospective or existing aquatic or riparian resources.
Because canyons and drainages are areas most frequented by wildlife species and because
drainages are also valuable components of the watershed, care will be taken to establish
vegetative buffer zones at the head of drainages and along ridge tops to enhance raptor
habitat and provide for watershed integrity. Fuel reduction efforts in primary canyons
and drainages would focus on reducing mixed conifer and heavy fuel loads.

Trt_Concerns_Desc:
The overall goals of this fuels management project are the prevention of stand-replacement wildland fires, the protection of the health and safety of the public and firefighters, the protection of the wildland/urban interface (WUI) and the health and productivity of the watershed, as well as the improvement of habitat for wildlife by creating more vegetative diversity. Treatment objectives include promoting successful regeneration of aspen stands, thinning coniferous trees and brush to a more natural and historic density, reducing fuels loads, enhancing wildlife habitat by reducing slash, brush and other understory vegetation in ponderosa pine/Douglas fir stands, and eventually reintroducing fire into the ecosystem to sustain a healthy forest.
The project will reduce
vegetative fuels and implement vegetative/habitat restoration activities within an approximate
6,840-acre project area of public lands administered by the BLM. The underlying need for the
proposal will be met while accomplishing the following objectives:
1.) Improve ecosystem function and restore vegetative resilience to facilitate recovery from
wildland fire. Because watershed health involves the combined workings of a watershed
such as land use, soils, and vegetation, the long-term objectives of this restoration
treatment are relevant to all of these resources.
2.) Enhance and expand declining aspen stands by reducing conifer density and
reintroducing fire into the ecosystem; improving soils, increasing forage and improving
habitat for wildlife and livestock while preventing and discouraging the spread of
invasive plant species.
3.) Protect the Wildland Urban Interface (WUI), wildlife habitat, and other resources in the
area from a severe, high intensity wildland fire while improving habitat diversity,
resiliency, and vigor.
The goals and objectives of the fuels reduction effort would
be to enhance public and firefighter safety and an increased range of suppression strategies. In
addition, a successful treatment would restore ecosystem health by reproducing the natural
variability, stability, and diversity of the vegetative communities within the project area.

Objectives: Reduce targeted pinyon/juniper stands and dense brush
Planned_Implementation:
Mechanical Treatment
Where soils are deeper and at higher elevations where moisture is more favorable to tree
growth there are stands of extremely dense pinyon-juniper growth. There are also high-top
medium-dense stands on the margins of the original chainings. Dense pinyon-juniper
presents a challenge both from a fuel hazard perspective and as an impediment to
restoration. Crown fire potential in these areas is significant because of canopy closure
along with an abundance of dead woody fuels remaining on the surface from the original
chaining. In accessible dense stands with flat terrain and in areas where rocky outcrops
are minimal, a mechanical chipper/shredder or “bullhog” would be used to achieve
treatment goals. A bullhog “masticates” both green and dead trees as well as ladder
fuels, scattering the remaining chipped materials (mulch) over the ground and
redistributing the fuel load. Mulched material generated from bullhog treatments would
eventually decompose, although future follow-up treatment with prescribed fire could be
used in some areas to reach desired wildland fire condition. Units targeted for
mechanical treatment and treatment design would be determined through coordination
between the fuels staff and Price Field Office resource staff.
